This introduction section from Po-Jung Huang's 2025 article discusses the evolution and impact of RNA sequencing, particularly focusing on the advancements in single-cell RNA sequencing technologies for studying cellular heterogeneity in multicellular systems.

RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has been widely used for over a decade to investigate transcriptomes. It has firmly established itself as the dominant method for exploring RNA repertoires in various organisms. Recent advancements in single-cell capture and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) technologies have revolutionized the study of cellular heterogeneity within multicellular systems. This has fundamentally reshaped the landscape of transcriptome research and is gradually replacing traditional bulk tissue experiments. Given the vast potential of scRNA-seq technology, numerous computational packages have been created to analyze large-scale gene expression data derived from it. Seurat (R) [ 1 ] and Scanpy (Python) [ 2 ] are widely used packages for scRNA-seq analysis, offering functions for quality control, data normalization, cell clustering, differential gene expression analysis, and cell type annotation. However, their command-line interfaces may pose challenges for clinicians and biomedical researchers without computational expertise. Substantial efforts have been made to develop web-based and graphical interfaces for scRNA-seq analysis [ 3–5 ], extending the functionality of Seurat and Scanpy. However, these platforms are often constrained by limited support for diverse input formats and reduced capacity to handle large datasets, primarily due to network transfer bottlenecks and web server execution time limits. While Seurat and Scanpy provide foundational tools for identifying marker genes through differential expression analysis, their manual cell-type annotation process remains laborious and subjective.

metadata.title: ShinySC: An R/Shiny-based desktop application for seamless analysis of scRNA-Seq data
metadata.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables detailed profiling of cellular heterogeneity, but complex workflows and diverse data formats limit accessibility for clinicians and researchers without programming expertise. We introduce ShinySC , an R/Shiny-based desktop application designed to streamline comprehensive scRNA-seq analysis through an intuitive graphical interface. ShinySC supports various input formats, including 10x Genomics, Seurat, Scanpy, BD Rhapsody, and CellView. The tool integrates essential analytical procedures such as quality control, normalization, dimensionality reduction, clustering, marker gene identification, batch correction, differential expression analysis, and trajectory inference. Notably, ShinySC implements multiple automatic cell-type annotation methods—reference-based (SingleR), marker-based (ScType, scCATCH), and GPT-based (GPTCelltype)—with features for side-by-side comparison and manual label refinement. Benchmarking indicates robust performance for datasets containing up to 200,000 cells on standard desktop systems with 64 GB RAM, with analysis duration dependent on specific tasks and annotation methods. Demonstrative analyses of PBMC and interferon-stimulated datasets confirm ShinySC's efficacy in accurately annotating cell types and capturing condition-specific transcriptional dynamics. ShinySC provides a unified, user-friendly, and scalable platform for scRNA-seq analysis explicitly tailored for non-programming users. It surpasses existing limitations by accommodating multiple data formats, employing versatile annotation strategies, and generating high-quality, publication-ready figures. Available freely across Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms, ShinySC enhances the accessibility and reproducibility of single-cell transcriptomic research. http://tardis.cgu.edu.tw/ShinySC .

While Seurat and Scanpy provide foundational tools for identifying marker genes through differential expression analysis, their manual cell-type annotation process remains laborious and subjective. Automated annotation strategies have been developed to overcome these limitations, broadly categorized into reference-based [ 6–8 ] and marker-based [ 9–15 ] approaches. Reference-based methods annotate cell types by leveraging transcriptome-wide correlations between query cells and well-annotated reference datasets. In contrast, marker-based methods assign cell-type labels based on curated databases of known marker genes, making them suitable for scenarios where tissue-matched reference datasets are unavailable. Recent AI advances have led to the development of GPTCelltype [ 9 ], an R package powered by GPT-4 that automates cell-type annotation with high accuracy, expert-level concordance, and superior efficiency. It has been proven effective in accurately identifying ambiguous or poorly characterized cell types and has the potential to integrate with Seurat workflows in a reference-free manner. However, most automated cell-type annotation tools are command-line-based. Although some provide web interfaces, they are typically constrained by specific data formats and file size limitations. Inconsistent output formats also hinder the direct comparison of different annotation tools.

ShinySC incorporates three annotation strategies across four algorithms for automatic cell type identification in scRNA-seq analysis: (1) reference-based annotation using SingleR [ 6 ], leveraging seven curated reference datasets, including HumanPrimaryCellAtlasData (HPCA), BlueprintEncodeData, DatabaseImmuneCellExpressionData (DICE), NovershternHematopoieticData, and MonacoImmuneData for human cells, and MouseRNAseqData and ImmGenData for mouse cells; (2) marker-based annotation through ScType [ 10 ], utilizing PanglaoDB [ 15 ] and CellMarker databases [ 33 ] across 15 tissue types with expression specificity scoring, and scCATCH [ 11 ], covering 353 cell types from 184 tissues based on CellMatch's evidence-based scoring system; and (3) GPT-4-based annotation via GPTCelltype [ 9 ], enabling contextual reasoning to infer cell identities.

Benchmarking of ShinySC was performed on an AMD Ryzen 7 1700 CPU with 64 GB RAM using datasets ranging from 2000 to 200,000 cells. These subsets were derived from a 320,000-cell human PBMC dataset generated with the GEM-X Flex platform using a 16-plex sub-pooling strategy, available from 10x Genomics [ Table S1 ]. Preprocessing (QC and normalization) and identifying highly variable genes were efficient and completed within approximately 1 min, even at larger cell counts. Computationally intensive tasks such as regression, PCA, clustering, and UMAP scaled linearly with dataset size, with regression being the most demanding (16.24 min for 200,000 cells). Differential gene expression analysis (FindAllMarkers) was the most time-consuming, peaking at 37.91 min for 200,000 cells but significantly faster at smaller scales. Annotation efficiency varied notably by the method: GPTCelltype annotation was exceptionally fast (under 1 min), ScType and SingleR remained efficient (1.50 and 6.49 min at 200,000 cells, respectively), whereas scCATCH required substantial computational resources (896.73 min at 200,000 cells). ShinySC demonstrated robust performance and scalability for handling large single-cell datasets, depending on task complexity and chosen annotation methods.

### ShinySC compared to other programs

[ Table S2 ] compares tools with features similar to ShinySC, including Azimuth [ 35 ], CITEViz [ 36 ], SCHNAPPs [ 37 ], iSEE [ 38 ], Single Cell Virtual Cytometer [ 39 ], Cerebro [ 40 ], and ScRNAPip [ 41 ]. ScRNAPip [ 41 ] can process FASTQ files but lacks built-in visualization and relies on Cerebro for result exploration, which complicates the workflow and reduces workflow continuity.
